newsitem.title: USA: DPUC blasts Conn. Yankee closing costs.
newsitem.headline: DPUC blasts Conn. Yankee closing costs.

text.p: Connecticut's legal chief and utilities regulator said Wednesday they have urged federal regulators to prevent the collection of additional funds for the dismantling of the Connecticut Yankee nuclear plant.
The 582-megawatt Connecticut Yankee plant in Haddam, Conn., was operated and 49-percent owned by Northeast Utilities, with the balance owned by seven other New England utilities.
It was shut down in July 1996 for safety reasons, and permanently closed last December.

The Department of Public Utility Control (DPUC) and Attorney General Richard Blumenthal on Tuesday filed testimony with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in which they said the plant closed because of mismanagement.
They said that the imprudent management led to additional costs which could have been avoided.
In addition, they charged that Connecticut Yankee's cost estimates for dismantling were largely speculative, and were inflated by as much as $220 million.

Connecticut Yankee's owners are asking the FERC to collect some $427 million for the decommissioning. About half of that amount has already been collected from Connecticut ratepayers, in the form of built-in decommissioning costs that came in when the plant was operational.
"This is another inflated request to grab ratepayer dollars," Blumenthal said. "No additional costs associated with the shutdown of Connecticut Yankee should be borne by Connecticut consumers."
Blumenthal and the DPUC said that if the FERC accepts their position, Connecticut ratepayers will save about $90 million.

In a separate development, the Connecticut Office of Consumer Counsel (OCC) said it has found "numerous and significant examples of imprudent management by Northeast Utilities" and its subsidiary, Connecticut Light & Power Co., in the operation of the Millstone and Connecticut Yankee plants.
Northeast's three Millstone nuclear plants in Waterford, Conn., have been closed for safety reasons since March 1996.
The OCC has already asked that ratepayers not be required to pay any part of the replacement power and repair costs stemming from the nuclear shutdowns.
Northeast has projected its nuclear outage-related costs at $990 million through 1998. It has not specified how much money it will seek to recover from ratepayers.
